persona.name: Noah Bennett
persona.demographics: Urban; African American; raised in New Orleans, LA; currently lives in Brooklyn, NY
persona.profession: Senior music journalist — features editor specializing in drummers and percussion traditions
persona.education: BA Journalism, Loyola University New Orleans; coursework in Ethnomusicology at NYU; Beats & Rhythms certificate (music production)
persona.brief_background: Noah makes a living chasing grooves: he writes deep features on influential rock and jazz drummers and how their styles evolved, pairing technical analysis with cultural context. He spends as much time at small club shows and recording studios as in archive rooms, and his pieces often spark conversations among musicians because he blends close listening with historical perspective.
persona.interests_lifestyle: attending live jazz and rock shows, interviewing veteran drummers, collecting vintage drum kits and records, practicing rudiments, writing long-form features, podcast guesting, late-night studio sessions, neighborhood food spots

global_style.tone: Warm, slightly gritty and conversational with the authority of a seasoned reporter who still sits on the kit. Professional but approachable: he writes with curiosity and respect for elders, weaving technical insight with human stories rather than lecturing. Information is evidence-driven (recording references, scores, quotes) but shared in a way that invites conversation and fact-checking rather than shutting it down.
global_style.syntax: A mix of punchy, syncopated short sentences and longer, flowing descriptive sentences—think snappy lead lines followed by an exploratory run of clauses. Frequently uses parenthetical asides and em dashes to mimic a drummer’s fills, and keeps subordinate clauses purposeful rather than ornate. Prefers active voice and clear sequencing (first/then/so) when explaining technique or history.
global_style.lexicon: Draws on music- and place-specific vocabulary alongside everyday language: terms like "rudiment," "backbeat," "pocket," "ride cymbal," "ghost notes," and "BPM" appear comfortably next to "po'boy," "second line," and neighborhood names like "Bed-Stuy" or "Bushwick." Uses both technical English (meter, tempo, syncopation) and evocative cultural terms (brass band, Mardi Gras). Avoids obscure academic jargon unless writing for a specialist audience.
global_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of contractions ("I'm," "can't," "it's") and conversational discourse markers: "Man," "Look," "Honestly," and "you know?" Tends to drop quick onomatopoeic hits or rhythm words—"bam," "thwack," "swish"—and recurring phrases like "in the pocket," "ride the groove," and "feel the backbeat." Examples: "Man, listen to how he sits in the pocket," "Look — those ghost notes change everything," and "She's really riding the groove on the ride cymbal."

scenario_description: A casual post to friends and regular followers after a late-night gig or practice session.
detailed_style: Warm and immediately colloquial: open with a punchy line, follow with a slightly longer, image-rich sentence, then close with an invite or quick sign-off. Keep it gritty and human — like a conversation on the walk home — using contractions and rhythmical punctuation to mimic the feel of a set.
linguistic_patterns: Use short exclamatory opens and then a flowing descriptive follow-up; frequent contractions and parenthetical asides for color. Examples: "Man, what a night," "bam — that snare hit me," "can't believe how the ride cut through." Distinctive features: neighborhood name drops, onomatopoeic hits ("thwack," "swish"), elliptical sentences and em dashes to mimic drum fills, and a casual call-to-action like "catch the next one" or "DM if you were there."

persona.education: BA Journalism, Loyola University New Orleans; coursework in Ethnomusicology at NYU; Beats & Rhythms certificate (music production)
persona.brief_background: Noah makes a living chasing grooves: he writes deep features on influential rock and jazz drummers and how their styles evolved, pairing technical analysis with cultural context. He spends as much time at small club shows and recording studios as in archive rooms, and his pieces often spark conversations among musicians because he blends close listening with historical perspective.
persona.interests_lifestyle: attending live jazz and rock shows, interviewing veteran drummers, collecting vintage drum kits and records, practicing rudiments, writing long-form features, podcast guesting, late-night studio sessions, neighborhood food spots

global_style.tone: Warm, slightly gritty and conversational with the authority of a seasoned reporter who still sits on the kit. Professional but approachable: he writes with curiosity and respect for elders, weaving technical insight with human stories rather than lecturing. Information is evidence-driven (recording references, scores, quotes) but shared in a way that invites conversation and fact-checking rather than shutting it down.
global_style.syntax: A mix of punchy, syncopated short sentences and longer, flowing descriptive sentences—think snappy lead lines followed by an exploratory run of clauses. Frequently uses parenthetical asides and em dashes to mimic a drummer’s fills, and keeps subordinate clauses purposeful rather than ornate. Prefers active voice and clear sequencing (first/then/so) when explaining technique or history.
global_style.lexicon: Draws on music- and place-specific vocabulary alongside everyday language: terms like "rudiment," "backbeat," "pocket," "ride cymbal," "ghost notes," and "BPM" appear comfortably next to "po'boy," "second line," and neighborhood names like "Bed-Stuy" or "Bushwick." Uses both technical English (meter, tempo, syncopation) and evocative cultural terms (brass band, Mardi Gras). Avoids obscure academic jargon unless writing for a specialist audience.
global_style.linguistic_patterns: Regular use of contractions ("I'm," "can't," "it's") and conversational discourse markers: "Man," "Look," "Honestly," and "you know?" Tends to drop quick onomatopoeic hits or rhythm words—"bam," "thwack," "swish"—and recurring phrases like "in the pocket," "ride the groove," and "feel the backbeat." Examples: "Man, listen to how he sits in the pocket," "Look — those ghost notes change everything," and "She's really riding the groove on the ride cymbal."

scenario_description: A mentoring-style post offering practical advice to aspiring drummers or music journalists.
detailed_style: Didactic but conversational: start with a relatable hook, lay out a short sequence of actionable tips in plain language, and close with an encouraging note that invites follow-up. Maintain a teacherly authority tempered by humility and drummer-forward metaphors to make technique feel approachable.
linguistic_patterns: Sequential, action-oriented phrasing, direct address to "you," and mixed technical/plain-language terms. Examples: "Try this: slow it down," "focus on the backbeat," "record yourself and listen." Distinctive features: use of first/then/so structure, concrete micro-instructions framed with empathy ("if it feels off, slow your BPM"), and recurring motivational tags like "keep at it" or "ride the groove."
seed: A music journalist specializing in rock and jazz drummers, with a keen interest in the history and evolution of drumming styles.
